claim: The neural data set used to fit 3D spatio-temporal models consisted of the average temporal response profile (PSTH) of each neuron for 26 directions of translation corresponding to all possible combinations of azimuth and elevation angles in increments of 45°.
source: The neural data set used to fit 3D spatio-temporal models consisted of the average temporal response profile (PSTH) of each neuron for 26 directions of translation corresponding to all possible combinations of azimuth and elevation angles in increments of 45° (Gu et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the composition of the neural data set used for modeling, including the number of directions and angular increments.

claim: The temporal waveform of the translational stimulus followed a Gaussian velocity profile with corresponding biphasic acceleration and triphasic jerk components.
source: The temporal waveform of the translational stimulus followed a Gaussian velocity profile (Figure 1, top), with corresponding biphasic acceleration (Figure 1, middle) and triphasic jerk (derivative of acceleration; Figure 1, bottom) components.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus characteristics and references Figure 1 which shows these temporal profiles.

claim: The data set included 27 otolith afferents, 49 VN cells, 61 CN cells, 115 PIVC cells, 66 VPS cells, 139 MSTd cells, 62 VIP cells, and 57 FEF cells.
source: This inclusion criterion yielded a total of 27 otolith afferents (OA), 49 VN cells, 61 CN cells, 115 PIVC cells (from Chen et al., 2010), 66 VPS cells (Chen et al., 2011b), 139 MSTd cells (from Gu et al., 2006), 62 VIP cells (from Chen et al., 2011c) and 57 FEF cells (from Gu et al., 2016) (see Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of neurons analyzed from each brain region.

claim: Otolith afferents carry spatially aligned cosine-tuned translational acceleration and jerk signals.
source: We demonstrate a remarkable spatio-temporal transformation: otolith afferents carry spatially aligned cosine-tuned translational acceleration and jerk signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Brainstem and cerebellar neurons exhibit non-linear, mixed selectivity for translational velocity, acceleration, jerk and position.
source: In contrast, brainstem and cerebellar neurons exhibit non-linear, mixed selectivity for translational velocity, acceleration, jerk and position.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The velocity, acceleration, jerk, and position components in brainstem and cerebellar neurons often show dissimilar spatial tuning.
source: Furthermore, these components often show dissimilar spatial tuning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding about central neurons.

claim: Moderate further transformation of translation signals occurs in the cortex, such that similar spatio-temporal properties are found in multiple cortical areas.
source: Moderate further transformation of translation signals occurs in the cortex, such that similar spatio-temporal properties are found in multiple cortical areas.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The first synapse represents a key processing element in vestibular pathways, robustly shaping how self-motion is represented in central vestibular circuits and cortical areas.
source: These results suggest that the first synapse represents a key processing element in vestibular pathways, robustly shaping how self-motion is represented in central vestibular circuits and cortical areas.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the observed transformations.

claim: Primary otolith afferents are spatially cosine-tuned and their temporal dynamics encode translational acceleration.
source: Primary otolith afferents are spatially cosine-tuned and their temporal dynamics are broadly thought to encode translational acceleration (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a, 1976b, 1976c; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Jamali et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Spatio-temporal convergence of otolith afferents onto central VN cells results in complex, non-cosine-tuned properties where spatial and temporal coding might not always be multiplicatively separable.
source: It has been proposed that spatio-temporal convergence of otolith afferents onto central VN cells results in complex, non-cosine-tuned properties, where spatial and temporal coding might not always be multiplicatively separable (Angelaki, 1991, 1992b; Angelaki et al., 1992; Angelaki, 1993; Angelaki et al., 1993; Bush et al., 1993; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010).
evidence: This statement cites prior theoretical and experimental work proposing this transformation.

claim: Model fits were generally good with median R2 values of 0.78 for OA, 0.65 for VN, 0.64 for CN, 0.71 for PIVC, 0.67 for VPS, 0.59 for MSTd, 0.66 for VIP, and 0.59 for FEF.
source: Model fits were generally good (Figure 4A), with median R2 values of 0.78 for OA (CI=[0.67–0.88]), 0.65 for VN (CI=[0.59–0.73]), 0.64 for CN (CI=[0.57–0.68]), 0.71 for PIVC (CI=[0.67–0.75]), 0.67 for VPS (CI=[0.62–0.71]), 0.59 for MSTd (CI=[0.55–0.64]), 0.66 for VIP (CI=[0.59–0.66]) and 0.59 for FEF (CI=[0.52–0.66]).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative goodness-of-fit measures for the models across all brain regions.

claim: Forty-eight percent of OAs were best fit by the A model and 33% by the AJ model, whereas only 19% were best fit by the VAJ model.
source: Forty-eight percent of OAs were best fit by the A model and 33% by the AJ model, whereas only 19% were best fit by the VAJ model.
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of best-fitting models for otolith afferents.

claim: For central cells, 6% were best fit by the V model, 20% and 10% by the VA and VJ model, and 60% by the VAJ model.
source: In contrast, 6% of central cells were best fit by the V model, 20% and 10% by the VA and VJ model, and 60% by the VAJ model, indicating that velocity responses were very common in central neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of best-fitting models for central neurons.

claim: In OAs, acceleration had high partial R2 values (median: 0.51), while the jerk and velocity contributions were small (median partial R2: 0.07 and 0.03, respectively).
source: In OAs, acceleration had high partial R2 values (median: 0.51, CI=[0.36–0.61]), while the jerk and velocity contributions were small (median partial R2: 0.07, CI=[0.02–0.13] and 0.03, CI=[0.02–0.06], respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measures of component contributions for otolith afferents.

claim: In central neurons, the velocity contribution was greatest (median partial R2: 0.38), followed by acceleration and jerk (median partial R2: 0.23 and 0.14, respectively).
source: In central neurons, the velocity contribution was greatest (median partial R2: 0.38, CI=[0.35–0.4]), followed by acceleration and jerk (median partial R2 : 0.23, CI=[0.21–0.25] and 0.14, CI=[0.13–0.15], respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measures of component contributions for central neurons.

claim: 'A' afferents had a lower normalized coefficient of variation CV* than 'AJ/VAJ' afferents (median 0.026 versus 0.06).
source: In particular 'A' afferents had a lower normalized coefficient of variation CV* (Goldberg et al., 1984) than 'AJ/VAJ' afferents (median 0.026, CI=[0.024–0.033] versus 0.06, CI=[0.04–0.08], Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=10−3; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in firing regularity between afferent types.

claim: The higher the CV* in otolith afferents, the higher the weights for velocity, acceleration and jerk.
source: We also found that the higher the CV* the higher the weights for velocity, acceleration and jerk (WV−green, WA-red, WJ-blue; Figure 5B, Spearman's rank correlation p<10−2 for all three variables), as response gain increases with CV*.
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant correlation between CV* and component weights.

claim: The contribution of velocity remained minimal in otolith afferents (median = 0.06) and did not correlate with CV*.
source: In contrast, the contribution of velocity remained minimal (median = 0.06, CI=[0.05–0.08]) and did not correlate with CV* (Spearman's rank correlation, p=0.75; Figure 5C, green).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of correlation between velocity contribution and CV* in otolith afferents.

claim: The preferred directions of the acceleration and jerk components were always aligned for OAs with a median angular difference of 7°.
source: The preferred directions for acceleration and jerk are aligned in all afferents that are tuned to these components (Figure 7D; see also Figure 5D, black).
evidence: The manuscript reports the alignment of preferred directions for acceleration and jerk in otolith afferents.

claim: The normalized acceleration weight is significantly smaller for VN and CN neurons compared to otolith afferents (p<10−8).
source: Quantitatively (see Table 2), the normalized acceleration weight (Figure 6E), which is high for otolith afferents, becomes significantly smaller for VN and CN neurons (p<10−8, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in acceleration weights between afferents and central neurons.

claim: The velocity weights are significantly greater for VN and CN neurons compared to otolith afferents (p<10−14).
source: In parallel, the velocity weights (Figure 6D) are significantly greater for VN and CN neurons, as compared to otolith afferents (p<10−14, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in velocity weights between afferents and central neurons.

claim: There is no significant difference between weight values for VN and CN areas.
source: Remarkably, despite dramatic differences in the relative weighting of acceleration and velocity signals between central cells and otolith afferents, VN and CN have similar properties overall, and there is no significant difference between weight values for the two areas (Wilcoxon's rank sum test, wv: p=0.75; wa; p=0.47; wj: p=0.28).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of significant differences between VN and CN neurons.

claim: Visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF) have slightly greater velocity weight (median: 0.39) compared to areas without optic flow responsiveness (VN, CN, PIVC; median 0.32) (p<10−9).
source: The most noticeable difference among cortical areas is the slightly greater velocity weight in visual/vestibular multisensory areas (MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF; median: 0.39, CI=[0.38–0.41]), as compared to those without optic flow responsiveness (VN, CN, PIVC; median 0.32, CI=[0.31–0.35]) (Figure 6D, cold vs. warm colors, respectively; p<10−9, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in velocity weights between multisensory and non-multisensory areas.

claim: OAs that were fit with the AJ or VAJ models have very high separability indices (median 0.98).
source: OAs that were fit with the AJ or VAJ models (n = 14) generally have very high separability indices (median 0.98, CI=[0.97–0.99]), indicating that their strongest temporal components have similar preferred directions and spatial tuning.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative separability measures for otolith afferents.

claim: Central brain areas have overall lower separability indices (median 0.89) compared to otolith afferents (p<10−12).
source: In contrast, central brain areas have overall lower separability indices (median 0.89, CI=[0.88–0.9]; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<10−12).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in separability between afferents and central neurons.

claim: There was a significant difference between the separability indices of VN/CN (median 0.82) and cortical regions (median 0.9) (p<10−8).
source: Within central cells, we found a significant difference between the separability indices of VN/CN and cortical regions (median 0.82, [0.81 0.84] CI versus 0.9, [0.89 0.91] CI, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<10−8).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in separability between subcortical and cortical neurons.

claim: Otolith afferents had the smallest modulation amplitude (median = 10 spikes/s) compared to all other brain areas (median = 43 spikes/s for central neurons) (p=10−11).
source: Otolith afferents had the smallest modulation amplitude (peak-to-trough amplitude of the spatio-temporal response curves, computed from the VAJ model fit) as compared to all other brain areas (median = 10 spikes/s, CI=[8-18] for OA versus 43 spikes/s, CI=[41-46] for all central neurons, Wilcoxon rank sum test: p=10−11; Figure 8A).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in response amplitude between afferents and central neurons.

claim: VN, CN and PIVC neurons had greater aggregate modulation amplitude (median = 58 spikes/s) than visual/vestibular multisensory areas VPS, MSTd, VIP and FEF (median: 35 spikes/s) (p<10−13).
source: VN, CN and PIVC neurons were the most responsive (Figure 8A, warm colors), with aggregate modulation amplitude (median = 58 spikes/s, CI=[54-63]) greater than visual/vestibular multisensory areas VPS, MSTd, VIP and FEF (Figure 8A, cold colors; median: 35 spikes/s, CI=[33-39], Wilcoxon's rank sum test: p<10−13).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistically significant difference in response amplitude between vestibular and multisensory areas.

claim: Baseline firing rate (FR0) was greatest in otolith afferents (median = 72 spikes/s), intermediate in VN/CN (median = 45 spikes/s), and smallest in cortical areas (median = 12 spikes/s).
source: FRo, which was greatest in otolith afferents (median = 72 spikes/s, CI=[54-90], Figure 8B, brown), intermediate in VN/CN (median = 45 spikes/s, CI=[38-49], Figure 8B, yellow/orange), and smallest in cortical areas (median = 12 spikes/s, CI=[11-13], Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative baseline firing rates across brain regions.

claim: OAs mainly encode acceleration and jerk with cosine tuning, with offset parameters clustering around zero.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2, OAs mainly encode acceleration and jerk with cosine tuning. Accordingly, the offset parameters of the acceleration and jerk components cluster around zero for OAs (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the spatial tuning characteristics of otolith afferents.

claim: Jerk responses in central neurons exhibited positive offsets (median 0.49) comparable to velocity responses.
source: Finally, we found that jerk responses in central neurons also exhibited positive offsets (median 0.49, CI=[0.46 0.52]; Figure 9C) comparable to velocity responses.
evidence: The manuscript reports the offset characteristics of jerk components in central neurons.

claim: Many central neurons had significant position contributions: OA: 1/27 (4%), VN: 41/49 (84%), CN: 47/61 (77%), PIVC: 63/115 (55%), VPS: 51/69 (74%), MSTd: 108/139 (78%), VIP: 40/62 (65%), FEF: 45/57 (79%).
source: Many central neurons had significant position contributions (Figure 10A,B, filled symbols and bars): OA: 1/27 (4%), VN: 41/49 (84%), CN: 47/61 (77%), PIVC: 63/115 (55%), VPS: 51/69 (74%), MSTd: 108/139 (78%), VIP: 40/62 (65%), FEF: 45/57 (79%).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons with significant position responses across brain regions.

claim: The position contribution was larger in MSTd compared to PIVC and VIP.
source: In agreement with the findings of Chen et al. (2011c), the position contribution was larger in MSTd, as compared to PIVC and VIP (areas for which the distribution is significantly different from MSTd are indicated by stars; *p<0.01; **p<0.001; two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistically significant differences in position contributions between cortical areas.

claim: Central neurons encode jerk (the derivative of linear acceleration) as well as position (displacement).
source: Furthermore, central neurons also encode jerk (the derivative of linear acceleration), as well as position (displacement).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The observed increase in velocity contribution to the spatio-temporal properties of central cells was accompanied by the presence of non-linearities.
source: The observed increase in velocity contribution to the spatio-temporal properties of central cells, as compared to otolith afferents, was accompanied by the presence of non-linearities.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be mostly cosine-tuned like otolith afferents.
source: Whereas the linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be, like otolith afferents, mostly cosine-tuned, the velocity component included substantial omni-directional contributions, and jerk had intermediate properties.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The velocity component of central cells included substantial omni-directional contributions.
source: Whereas the linear acceleration component of central cells continued to be, like otolith afferents, mostly cosine-tuned, the velocity component included substantial omni-directional contributions, and jerk had intermediate properties.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Central neurons carry information about the direction of linear acceleration and also encode the presence or absence of translational motion without regard for direction.
source: Thus, central neurons, like afferents, continued to carry information about the direction of linear acceleration, but they also encoded another type of signal: the presence or absence of translational motion without regard for direction.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion section.

claim: The omnidirectional motion signal in central neurons cannot be characterized with steady-state sinusoidal stimuli.
source: This component, which was strong in both the cortex and vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, cannot be characterized with the steady-state sinusoidal stimuli that have traditionally been the stimuli of choice in the vestibular system.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings in the Discussion section.

claim: There were only moderate differences in the relative contributions of velocity, acceleration and jerk among central subcortical and cortical neurons.
source: In contrast to the large differences in the types of signals encoded by otolith afferents versus their target cells in the vestibular nuclei, we found only moderate differences in the relative contributions of velocity, acceleration and jerk among central subcortical (vestibular and cerebellar nuclei) and cortical neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Response amplitude to an identical stimulus was lowest in otolith afferents and greatest in vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, PIVC and VPS.
source: Furthermore, response amplitude to an identical stimulus was lowest in otolith afferents and greatest in vestibular/cerebellar nuclei, PIVC and VPS – the areas known to form the core of the central vestibular system (Angelaki et al., 2009; Lopez and Blanke, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Response amplitude is lower in MSTd, VIP and FEF, which are visual/vestibular multisensory areas.
source: In contrast, response amplitude is lower in MSTd, VIP and FEF, which are visual/vestibular multisensory areas.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The signal transformation between sensory afferents and their targets in the brainstem and cerebellum represents a key processing element in the vestibular system.
source: In summary, these results suggest that the signal transformation that takes place between sensory afferents and their targets in the brainstem and cerebellum represents a key processing element in the vestibular system.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Using identical passive stimuli, cortical areas show moderate differences compared to the response properties in the brainstem and cerebellum.
source: Using identical passive stimuli, cortical areas show moderate differences, as compared to the response properties in the brainstem and cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Afferents from a single otolith organ differ in both spatial and temporal response properties.
source: First, afferents from a single otolith organ differ in both spatial and temporal response properties (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a, 1976b, 1976c; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Yu et al., 2012; Jamali et al., 2013) and extensive convergence in the vestibular nuclei (Kushiro et al., 2000; Straka et al., 2002; Uchino et al., 2001; Uchino and Kushiro, 2011) creates complex spatio-temporal convergence properties (Angelaki et al., 1992; Bush et al., 1993; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010).
evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge from prior literature about otolith afferent properties.

claim: Otolith afferents cannot distinguish tilt relative to gravity from translational acceleration.
source: Second, otolith afferents cannot distinguish tilt relative to gravity from translational acceleration.
evidence: This statement describes a fundamental property of otolith afferents based on established knowledge.

claim: The tilt/translation ambiguity has been resolved in the cortex, where neurons selective for inertial (translational) accelerations are found in PIVC and MSTd.
source: However, this tilt/translation ambiguity has been resolved in the cortex, where neurons that are selective for inertial (translational) accelerations are found (PIVC: Liu et al., 2011; MSTd: Liu and Angelaki, 2009).
evidence: This statement cites prior work showing resolution of the tilt/translation ambiguity in cortex.

claim: The property of cortical neurons being selective for inertial accelerations is likely inherited from subcortical signals through otolith/canal convergence in the brainstem and cerebellum.
source: This property of cortical neurons is likely inherited from subcortical signals, as there is growing evidence that this computation is implemented through otolith/canal convergence in the brainstem and cerebellum (VN/CN: Angelaki et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013; caudal cerebellar vermis: Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This statement cites evidence for the neural mechanisms underlying tilt/translation disambiguation.

claim: It is possible that the large differences in spatio-temporal response properties between otolith afferents and VN/CN neurons arise from neural computations that resolve the tilt/translation ambiguity.
source: It is thus possible that the large differences in spatio-temporal response properties that we have found between otolith afferents and VN/CN neurons arise from neural computations that resolve the tilt/translation ambiguity, a vital and critically important function for spatial orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Otolith afferents have been previously characterized in terms of preferred direction in three-dimensions and response dynamics.
source: Otolith afferents have been previously characterized in terms of preferred direction in three-dimensions (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a; Tomko et al., 1981; Yu et al., 2012) and response dynamics (Anderson et al., 1978; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b; Goldberg et al., 1990; Si et al., 1997; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Purcell et al., 2003; Jamali et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior literature on otolith afferent characterization.

claim: The activity of each otolith afferent fiber is determined by the product of a temporal 'transfer' function and a cosine-tuned spatial function.
source: These two properties are separable, with the activity of each afferent fiber being determined by the product of a temporal 'transfer' function and a cosine-tuned spatial function (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976a, 1976b, 1976c).
evidence: This statement cites prior work establishing the separability of spatial and temporal properties in otolith afferents.

claim: Otolith afferents have the same response dynamics along different spatial directions as a result of spatio-temporal separability.
source: As a result of this separability, otolith afferents have the same response dynamics along different spatial directions.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the separability property.

claim: Otolith afferents differ in their response dynamics based upon the regularity of their spontaneous discharge.
source: It has long been recognized that otolith afferents differ in their response dynamics based upon the regularity of their spontaneous discharge (Anderson et al., 1978; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Blanks and Precht, 1978; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b, 1976c; Goldberg et al., 1990; Jamali et al., 2009, 2013; Purcell et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement summarizes established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: The most regular otolith afferents encoded pure acceleration, whereas more irregular afferents encoded mixtures of acceleration and jerk.
source: Thus, the most regular afferents encoded pure acceleration, whereas more irregular afferents encoded mixtures of acceleration and jerk.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: The findings of phase leads and gain advances in less regularly-firing afferents are consistent with previous studies using sinusoidal stimulation.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies reporting phase leads and gain advances in less regularly-firing afferents during sinusoidal stimulation (Anderson et al., 1978; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Fernández and Goldberg, 1976b; Goldberg et al., 1990; Jamali et al., 2013; Purcell et al., 2003; Si et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement relates the current findings to prior literature.

claim: Less regular-firing otolith afferents included a small but consistent velocity component whose preferred direction relative to jerk and acceleration components is correlated with CV*.
source: Less regular-firing afferents also included a small but consistent velocity component, whose preferred direction relative to that of the jerk and acceleration components is correlated with CV*.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding from the current study.

claim: The velocity component in less regular-firing afferents has not been described previously using sinusoidal stimulation.
source: Such a response component has not been described previously using sinusoidal stimulation.
evidence: This statement indicates the novelty of the velocity component finding.

claim: VN neurons receive extensive convergence from otolith afferents that vary in their 3D spatial and temporal properties.
source: Because VN neurons receive extensive convergence from otolith afferents that vary in their 3D spatial and temporal properties, a computational challenge arises.
evidence: This statement describes the anatomical basis for the computational challenge.

claim: Theoretical analysis showed that central neurons receiving otolith afferent convergence should exhibit spatio-temporal convergence properties where spatial and temporal coding might not necessarily be separable.
source: Theoretical analysis of such convergence showed that central neurons receiving otolith afferent convergence should, in general, exhibit spatio-temporal convergence properties, where spatial and temporal coding might not necessarily be separable; this results in complex spatial (non-cosine-tuned) properties, where central neurons carry different proportions of velocity, acceleration and jerk signals along different spatial directions (Angelaki, 1992a, 1992b, 1992c; Schor and Angelaki, 1992; Angelaki et al., 1993; Angelaki and Dickman, 2000).
evidence: This statement cites prior theoretical work predicting non-separable properties in central neurons.

claim: Evidence for simultaneous coding of both translational acceleration and jerk was demonstrated in VN responses of decerebrate rodents.
source: Evidence for simultaneous coding of both translational acceleration and jerk was indeed demonstrated in VN responses of decerebrate rodents (Angelaki et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement cites prior experimental evidence supporting the theoretical predictions.

claim: Some experimental evidence for spatio-temporal convergence properties was provided for neurons in the primate VN and CN.
source: It took several more years until some experimental evidence for spatio-temporal convergence properties was provided for neurons in the primate VN (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010) and CN (Shaikh et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites prior experimental work on primate VN and CN neurons.

claim: All previously published studies of responses of VN/CN neurons to translation used sinusoidal stimuli.
source: However, to our knowledge, all previously published studies of responses of VN/CN neurons to translation used sinusoidal stimuli.
evidence: This statement characterizes the limitations of prior experimental approaches.

claim: VN and CN responses are characterized by non-minimum phase properties, complicating identification of temporal dynamics using sinusoids.
source: First, VN and CN responses are characterized by non-minimum phase properties, i.e., phase and gain changes do not parallel each other, thus complicating identification of temporal dynamics using sinusoids (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Shaikh et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites prior work identifying limitations of sinusoidal stimuli for characterizing VN/CN responses.

claim: Responses proportional to the temporal derivative and integral of translational acceleration cannot be easily separated using sinusoidal stimuli.
source: Second, responses proportional to the temporal derivative and integral of translational acceleration cannot be easily separated using sinusoidal stimuli (e.g., a phase difference of 90° relative to acceleration could reflect either velocity coding in one direction or jerk coding in the opposite direction).
evidence: This statement explains a fundamental limitation of sinusoidal stimuli.

claim: The traditional approach of testing sinusoidal responses at different frequencies to distinguish velocity from jerk contributions is complicated by non-minimum phase properties.
source: The traditional approach of testing sinusoidal responses at different frequencies to distinguish velocity from jerk contributions using linear systems analyses is complicated by the presence of non-minimum phase properties, thus making system identification challenging (Angelaki and Dickman, 2000; Dickman and Angelaki, 2002; Shaikh et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement explains why traditional frequency analysis approaches are problematic for VN/CN neurons.

claim: If response dynamics vary with stimulus direction, a complete characterization of spatio-temporal properties requires testing cells at multiple frequencies and multiple directions in 3D.
source: Furthermore, if indeed response dynamics vary with stimulus direction, a complete characterization of the spatio-temporal properties requires testing cells at multiple frequencies and multiple directions in 3D (Chen-Huang and Peterson, 2006, 2010).
evidence: This statement cites prior work that attempted comprehensive 3D characterization using sinusoids.

claim: Non-linearities in spatio-temporal tuning can violate the assumptions of traditional linear systems analysis.
source: Third, non-linearities in spatio-temporal tuning, as reported here (see also Chen et al., 2011c; Massot et al., 2012) can violate the assumptions of traditional linear systems analysis, thus rendering previous conclusions based on steady-state frequency analysis problematic.
evidence: This statement explains how non-linearities limit the validity of prior approaches.

claim: These limitations have been circumvented by the use of 3D transient stimuli and comparison of neural responses in multiple subcortical and cortical areas.
source: These limitations have been circumvented here, for the first time, by the use of 3D transient stimuli and a comparison of neural responses in multiple subcortical and cortical areas.
evidence: This statement describes the methodological innovation of the current study.

claim: With the exception of Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), nothing is known about spatio-temporal convergence in any brain region using transient stimuli.
source: With the exception of Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), who characterized 3D responses in the VN using sinusoidal stimuli (see limitations above), nothing is known about spatio-temporal convergence in any brain region using transient stimuli.
evidence: This statement emphasizes the novelty of the current approach.

claim: Understanding the full extent of underlying spatio-temporal computations is only achievable when data are analyzed in 3D.
source: Yet, as previously also emphasized by Chen-Huang and Peterson (2010), understanding the full extent of the underlying spatio-temporal computations is only achievable when data are analyzed in 3D, and conclusions drawn by characterizing responses along a single direction or within a single plane can be rather incomplete.
evidence: This statement emphasizes the importance of 3D analysis, citing prior work.

claim: The current findings provide the first quantification of 3D spatio-temporal convergence properties using transient stimuli along many spatial directions.
source: Our current findings have provided the first such quantification of 3D spatio-temporal convergence properties using transient stimuli along many spatial directions.
evidence: This statement emphasizes the novelty and significance of the current study.

claim: Most central cells show omni-directional tuning components.
source: Most central cells show omni-directional tuning components.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding about central neuron responses.

claim: The existence of broad or uniform tuning suggests that many afferents converge onto one central neuron.
source: The existence of broad or uniform tuning, as opposed to cosine tuning, suggests that many afferents converge onto one central neuron.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the broad tuning findings.

claim: Broadly tuned neurons respond to motion in directions that are orthogonal to their preferred direction.
source: Indeed, broadly tuned neurons respond to motion in directions that are orthogonal to their PD.
evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of broadly tuned neurons.

claim: In otolith afferents, all directions that are orthogonal to the preferred direction are null directions.
source: In contrast, in OA, all directions that are orthogonal to the PD are null directions.
evidence: This statement describes a characteristic of otolith afferent tuning.

claim: The transformation of responses from sensory afferents to brainstem neurons may be coupled to the resolution of the tilt/translation ambiguity.
source: These results suggest that the transformation of responses from sensory afferents to brainstem neurons represents a key processing element, possibly because it is coupled to the resolution of a tilt/translation ambiguity that represents a critically important function for spatial orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Theoretical solutions to the tilt/translation ambiguity problem require strong non-linearities.
source: Although there is no direct evidence yet for such a link, theoretical solutions to the ambiguity problem require strong non-linearities (Borah et al., 1988; Merfeld, 1995; Glasauer and Merfeld, 1997; Merfeld et al., 1999; Angelaki et al., 1999, 2004; Laurens and Droulez, 2007; Laurens and Angelaki, 2011).
evidence: This statement cites theoretical work on tilt/translation disambiguation.

claim: Mixed selectivity plays an important computational role by allowing high-dimensional representations that enable a simple linear readout to generate diverse responses.
source: It has been proposed that mixed selectivity plays an important computational role: high-dimensional representations with mixed selectivity allow a simple linear readout to generate a diverse array of potential responses (Fusi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement cites theoretical work on the computational role of mixed selectivity.

claim: Representations based on highly specialized neurons are low dimensional and may preclude a linear readout from generating several responses that depend on multiple task-relevant variables.
source: In contrast, representations based on highly specialized neurons are low dimensional and may preclude a linear readout from generating several responses that depend on multiple task-relevant variables.
evidence: This statement cites theoretical work contrasting specialized versus mixed selectivity representations.

claim: Complex non-linear operations can be performed by simple linear summations of non-linear neurons.
source: Complex non-linear operations can be performed by simple linear summations of non-linear neurons, and in turn linear summation may be easily learned by neuronal networks.
evidence: This statement describes a theoretical principle about neural computation.

claim: A rich variety of non-linearly transformed signals may facilitate the learning of complex computations.
source: Thus, a rich variety of non-linearly transformed signals may facilitate the learning of complex computations.
evidence: This statement presents a theoretical principle about neural computation.

claim: The spatio-temporal transformations in VN/CN might reflect the need to perform non-linear, three-dimensional spatio-temporal operations necessary to implement an internal model of head motion.
source: It is possible that the described spatio-temporal transformations in VN/CN might reflect the need to perform non-linear, three-dimensional spatio-temporal operations necessary to implement an internal model of head motion (Merfeld, 1995; Laurens and Angelaki, 2011), whose influence has been documented in subcortical neurons (Angelaki et al., 2004; Yakusheva et al., 2007; Laurens et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Complex spatio-temporal representations of movement may be passed on to cortical neurons to subserve their respective roles in spatial cognition.
source: Complex spatio-temporal representations of movement may be passed on to cortical (Liu and Angelaki, 2009; Liu et al., 2011) neurons to subserve their respective roles in spatial cognition.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Each movement trajectory consisted of a Gaussian velocity profile with total displacement of 13 cm and peak acceleration of 0.1 g.
source: Each movement trajectory consisted of a Gaussian velocity profile (0.2 s standard deviation) with corresponding biphasic acceleration and triphasic jerk profiles. The total displacement was 13 cm and the peak acceleration was 0.1 g.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: All movements originated from the center of the movement range of the motion platform, and the platform returned to this starting position during the 2 s inter-trial interval.
source: All movements originated from the center of the movement range of the motion platform, and the platform returned to this starting position during the 2 s inter-trial interval.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Otolith afferents, VN, CN and PIVC neurons are not sensitive to visual stimuli or eye movements.
source: Previous findings have established that otolith afferents, VN, CN and PIVC neurons are not sensitive to visual stimuli or eye movements (for details see Bryan and Angelaki, 2009; Liu et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites prior work establishing the lack of visual/eye movement sensitivity in these neurons.

claim: For MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF neurons, vestibular translation responses during fixation are similar to those in complete darkness.
source: For MSTd, VPS, VIP and FEF neurons, which are sensitive to eye movements and/or visual motion, we have previously verified that vestibular translation responses during fixation are similar to those in complete darkness (details and comparison figures can be found in: Gu et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2007 and Chowdhury et al., 2009 for MSTd, Chen et al., 2011a for VPS, Chen et al., 2011b for VIP and Gu et al., 2016 for FEF).
evidence: This statement cites prior work verifying that vestibular responses are similar in darkness and during fixation.
